newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Security Council extends Iraq oil-for-food deal.
newsitem.headline: Security Council extends Iraq oil-for-food deal.

text.p: The Security Council voted unanimously on Wednesday to approve a six-month renewal of its "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq to ease the plight of civilians under crippling U.N. sanctions for nearly seven years.

Under the plan, which took effect on Dec. 10 and expires on June 7, Iraq has been allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help alleviate the effects of embargoes in force since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The new council resolution, adopted in a brief two-minute meeting, would renew the arrangement for another 180-day period beginning at 12:01 a.m. EDT (0401 GMT) on June 8.

It says the council "expresses its intention, prior to the end of the 180-day period, to consider favourably renewal of the provisions of this resolution, provided that the reports ... indicate that those provisions are being satisfactorily implemented."
About two-thirds of the oil revenues are for humanitarian supplies, with the remainder earmarked for compensation of Gulf War victims and the costs of destroying Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.

A major preoccupation of the council has been to ensure that all sectors of the Iraqi population benefit from the supplies bought with the limited oil sales, not just groups favoured by the Baghdad government. U.N. observers have been deployed in the country to ensure this.

The resolution also says the council "expresses its intention, prior to the end of the 180-day period, to consider favourably renewal of the provisions of this resolution, provided that the reports ... indicate that those provisions are being satisfactorily implemented."

The United States and Britain said the United Nations needed to provide better information about the distribution of humanitarian goods under the "oil-for-food" deal. "We are not entirely satisfied with the implementation so far by the Iraqis and by the (U.N.) secretariat," U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson said.

"They need to provide better and more timely and accurate information, specifically on Iraqis' distribution methods, the operation in the north, and other implementation facets that are not, in our judgment, being properly handled."

He was referring to measures to ensure the fair distribution of humanitarian supplies among all sectors of the Iraqi population, both in the largely Kurdish-inhabited north where the United Nations is in charge of distribution and in the rest of the country, where Iraqi authorities are responsible, subject to U.N. monitoring.
Asked about any increase in the $2 billion worth of oil sales permitted under the deal, he replied; "We don't think that's needed."

British Ambassador Sir John Weston told reporters that "one of the points to which we attach importance is that there should be proper monitoring in the way these humanitarian supplies are distributed."

The resolution also directs the sanctions committee to "process expeditiously contract applications" submitted for the purchase of food and other supplies as soon as Annan has approved a new plan to be submitted by Iraq guaranteeing equitable distribution and describing items to be purchased.

Iraq has frequently complained that the sanctions committee, at the alleged instigation of the United States, has delayed approval of contracts for the purchase of humanitarian supplies. This led to a long delay before the goods began arriving in Iraq although arrangements for the sale of oil proceeded smoothly.

But a Clinton administration official said Washington was only following procedures that Iraq had demanded, such as Baghdad's signature on all goods contracts to make sure they were the proper ones. He did, however, say the United States had delayed non-food and medical contracts because the United Nations did not have enough monitors on the ground.
